content.text: is Swahili for 'research'. Tell us more about the fund.

The Newton-Utafiti Fund consists of multiple parties contributing to a single fund that provides a number of grants for the hosting of workshops, capacity building scholarships and primary research. The fund will give local scientists the opportunity to build academic relationships through joint research and is likely to be the beginning of long term partnerships among different researchers.
What was the AKU grant about?

We applied for a grant to host a workshop for 30 early career researchers who will address a subject of national interest: health systems that would support delivery of services for women, newborns and children. We are working on having the workshop sometime in September and it will most likely take place in Johannesburg, South Africa. This particular workshop will train early career researchers and facilitate introductions that can lead to joint research proposals being developed for external grants. It has been designed to generate two or three proposals in maternal, new born and child health that will be lodged for funding from different grants, either from Newton Fund or other sources.

As stipulated in the requirements of this grant, the research workshop must address areas of importance in the field of health research and our focus is on what the teams can contribute towards assisting Kenya and the other partner countries in attaining sustainable development.

Two years ago we conducted a study known as the Kenya: Countdown to 2015, which revealed wide disparities, for example, in coverage of childhood immunization, provision of services for family planning and also services to women and children. The study also discovered wide gaps in the nutritional status of children under the age of five. When there was a comparison of access to quality healthcare using specified indicators for rural and urban populations, the study revealed that rural populations are still disadvantaged.

Going forward, even as we expand coverage for a continuum of care - from pregnancy, to the time of birth and in children under the age of five - we have to be cognizant of the inequities that are still present in certain areas.
What would be the impact of the workshop and who are the main beneficiaries?

This particular workshop will train early career researchers and facilitate introductions that can lead to joint research proposals being developed for external grants. It has been designed to generate two or three proposals in maternal, newborn and child health that will be lodged for funding from different grants, either from Newton Fund or other sources. While the immediate beneficiaries may be these early career researchers, the ultimate winners will be the populations of the partnering countries.

The researchers would have the opportunity to be trained by highly skilled resource persons. We have Professor Marleen Temmerman, head of Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, and the director of the Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health in East Africa. She brings in a lot of experience from Ghent University in Belgium where she is a full Professor of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the World Health Organisation, Geneva, where she was the director of the Department of Reproductive Health and Research. Similarly, we have highly qualified individuals from the three partner countries. We also expect Professor Zulfiqar Bhutta, global Director, Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health to attend.

The participants will therefore have opportunity to listen to and be mentored by highly distinguished individuals and by the end of the workshop they will have developed new research knowledge and skills that they can implement.  For the populations in the partnering countries, the workshop will help attract funding aimed at addressing challenges related to women and child health.
Can you comment on the level of health research funding in Kenya?

Research funding has, over the years, been highly dependent on external funding. However, the Government has made provision for at least two percent of the GDP (gross domestic product) to be channeled towards research with effect from last year. This initial contribution by the National Health Research Fund towards supporting local research work through grants has been a huge milestone as it gives preference to Kenyan scientists. In the past it was a challenge as local researchers had to compete with their counterparts globally for grants.
What does the grant mean to you as a researcher and the Aga Khan University in East Africa?

This grant and several others that we have either won this year or have applied for and expect to get will open a new window of increased activities in health research. We have a very cohesive team of senior researchers with the knowhow of applying and effectively competing for grants and we look forward to interesting times in the next two or three years when we expect to see a rise in the number of awarded grants.
The University recently launched a research office in Mombasa. What are some of the issues you seek to address?

We received a five-year grant from the Canadian government for the improvement of women and child health in the Coast region and we needed offices from which we can co-ordinate our research activities. This grant has enabled us to expand and to undertake more ambitious projects that will have a regional impact.

content.title: Newton-Utafiti Fund
content.author: kennedy.njenga
content.description:
AKU's Faculty of Health Sciences in East Africa has won a grant from the Newton- Utafiti  Fund, a collaborative partnership to strengthen links in science and innovation between the UK and Kenya, to conduct a health research workshop that will bring together researchers from the two countries. 
    The 
    Newton- Utafiti  Fund  is part of the wider Newton Fund  family with Kenya becoming the 16th country to participate, joining two other countries on the continent Egypt and South Africa. In Kenya, the Fund is administered in partnership with the Kenyan Ministry of Education with funding from the National Council for Science, Technology and Innovation, the National Research Fund and the Kenya National Innovation Agency. 
    Professor William Macharia, head of research services at the Faculty of Health Sciences discloses the details.
